blocks.content: An anonymous volume is created implicitly, without a name, whenever a container mounts a volume path without you specifying one. They work the same as named volumes, but are much easier to lose track of.

Mounting a container path with -v /data (no name before the colon) or relying on a Dockerfile's VOLUME instruction without an explicit mount creates a volume automatically, Docker assigns it a long random hash instead of a name you chose.

blocks.alt: A random hash name, since none was given

blocks.content:
docker run -d -v /data myapp
# Creates an anonymous volume, something like:
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...long hash...

code.content:
docker run -d -v /data myapp
# Creates an anonymous volume, something like:
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...long hash...

codes.bash:
docker run -d -v /data myapp
# Creates an anonymous volume, something like:
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...long hash...

blocks.content: Because an anonymous volume has no memorable name, it is easy to lose track of entirely. Remove the container without thinking about its volumes, and the anonymous volume can linger on disk indefinitely, invisible and unreferenced, quietly consuming space.

blocks.alt: Forgotten volumes can pile up, unnoticed, over time

blocks.content: Adding -v to docker rm tells Docker to remove any anonymous volumes that were attached to that specific container at the same time, a named volume attached the same way is left untouched, only anonymous ones are swept up.

blocks.alt: A cleanup flag scoped specifically to anonymous volumes

blocks.content:
docker rm -v mycontainer
# Removes the container AND any anonymous volumes it had,
# named volumes it used are left alone.

code.content:
docker rm -v mycontainer
# Removes the container AND any anonymous volumes it had,
# named volumes it used are left alone.

codes.bash:
docker rm -v mycontainer
# Removes the container AND any anonymous volumes it had,
# named volumes it used are left alone.

blocks.content: For volumes that have already been orphaned, docker volume prune removes every volume (named or anonymous) that is not currently attached to any container, a useful periodic cleanup command on a machine that has accumulated cruft over time.

blocks.alt: A bulk cleanup for anything no longer in use

blocks.content:
docker volume prune
# Removes all volumes not currently used by at least one container.

code.content:
docker volume prune
# Removes all volumes not currently used by at least one container.

codes.bash:
docker volume prune
# Removes all volumes not currently used by at least one container.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Anonymous volumes are created automatically when a volume path is mounted without a name, and are much easier to lose track of than named ones.
docker rm -v cleans up anonymous volumes tied to that container, docker volume prune sweeps up any orphaned volume left behind, named or not.
